summary: Discusses the concept of network intents, high-level abstract policies used to operate a network, and also considers other types of intents. It covers perspectives of different stakeholders and classifies intents. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Intent is a wish like make the network fast for class time. This sorts those wishes into groups by who is asking and what they want.

questions: what are the types of network intent
what is intent for different stakeholders
subtitle: How to categorize and understand different types of network intent

tldr.problem: Intent-based networking has become an active area, but different stakeholders (carriers, data centers, enterprises) use intent in different ways. There is no shared understanding of what intent types, users, and categories exist across different network domains.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC proposes an intent classification methodology based on solution knowledge, then applies it to derive taxonomies for three domain solutions: carrier networks, data center networks, and enterprise networks. For each, it identifies intent users, intent types, scope, abstraction level, and lifecycle requirements.
tldr.outcome: Researchers and developers can now classify intent-based demos, tools, and solutions consistently, facilitating comparison and advancing the field.

facts.label: Three primary solution domains
facts.value: Carrier networks, data center networks, enterprise networks

facts.value: Solution, intent users, intent types, scope, network scope, abstraction, lifecycle

today: RFC 9316 is Informational and produced by the IRTF Network Management Research Group. It is used by researchers and practitioners to classify intent-based systems, verify that new approaches address recognized intent categories, and identify gaps in current solutions. The taxonomy is designed to be extended as new domains and scenarios emerge.

sections.title: Intent Across Different Domains
sections.content:
Intent-based networking is gaining attention in research and industry, but different domains approach intent differently. A carrier network operator asking for intent has different concerns than a data center administrator or an enterprise IT manager. Yet all use the term "intent," creating confusion about what they actually mean.

This RFC tackles that problem by proposing a classification methodology and taxonomy that clarifies what intent means in different contexts. The document is a product of the IRTF Network Management Research Group (NMRG) and reflects consensus from researchers and practitioners working on intent-driven systems.

The approach is intentionally expandable: while the RFC focuses on carrier, data center, and enterprise solutions, the methodology can be applied to other domains as they emerge. The goal is to provide a foundation that helps researchers propose new intent languages, verify intent systems, and develop solutions that address different stakeholder needs.
sections.eli5: Different people use "intent" to mean different things depending on what they're trying to do. A telecom company managing thousands of customer connections thinks about intent differently than a company managing a data center or an office network. This explains what each one means.

sections.title: Intent Requirements and Solutions
sections.content:
Intent requirements vary based on the solution and the intent users involved. The RFC identifies key dimensions for classifying intent:

Intent Users differ across solutions. In carrier networks, users include customers/subscribers, network operators, and service designers. In data centers, users include cloud administrators, underlay network administrators, and application developers. In enterprises, users include enterprise administrators, application developers, and end users.

Intent Types describe what is being managed. These include customer service intent (customer-facing SLA-based service), network service intent (service operator perspective), network intent (network-wide configuration and resource management), operational task intent (network migrations, device replacements), strategy intent (policies and workflows that guide other intents), and for data centers, cloud management intent and cloud resource management intent.

Intent Scope defines what aspect of the network or service is affected: connectivity, application, QoS, security/privacy, storage (for data centers), or compute (for data centers).

Network Scope identifies which part of the network is targeted: radio access, branches, transport networks, data center segments, campus networks, or cloud environments.

Abstraction Level determines whether intent users receive technical feedback about how the intent was achieved (for technical administrators) or only whether it worked (for non-technical users).

Intent Lifecycle classifies intent as either transient (accomplished once and finished) or persistent (actively maintained until explicitly withdrawn).
sections.eli5: Intent can be about different things (service, network, strategy), aimed at different people (operators, developers, customers), affect different parts of the network (access, core, cloud), and work differently (tell me technical details or just say it's done, keep it running forever or just do it once).

sections.title: Classification Methodology
sections.content:
The RFC proposes an eight-step methodology for classifying intent in any solution. The process starts from solution knowledge (requirements, use cases, technologies, intent users involved) and systematically identifies:

1. The intent solution (carrier, data center, enterprise, or new domains)

2. The intent user types involved in that solution

3. The types of intent each user requires

4. The scopes (connectivity, security, application, etc.) addressed by each intent type

5. The network scopes (which network segments are targeted)

6. The abstraction levels (technical feedback or non-technical)

7. The lifecycle requirements (transient or persistent)

8. Any new categories not yet covered

At each step, the methodology recommends reviewing existing classifications to see whether categories already exist, can be reused, should be extended, or should be removed. This keeps the taxonomy consistent while allowing it to grow as new scenarios emerge.
sections.eli5: Here's how you figure out what kind of intent you're dealing with: first, what domain is it (carrier, data center, etc.)? Who is asking (a customer or an administrator)? What do they want (a service, network changes, or a rule)? What part of the network? Should they see technical details? Will it be temporary or permanent? Any other unique aspect?

sections.title: Intent Taxonomy for Different Domains
sections.content:
Applying the methodology yields distinct taxonomies for each solution type.

For carrier networks, customer/subscribers want customer service intent (gold-level bandwidth guarantees, for example). Network operators manage network service intent (delivering services with delay guarantees), network intent (routing, QoS, security policies), and operational task intent (migrations, device replacements). Operators also design strategy intent that guides how other intents are achieved.

For data center networks, cloud administrators manage cloud management intent (VM configuration and communication), cloud resource management intent (auto-scaling, recovery), and service-level intent. Network administrators manage underlay network service intent and network intent. The scope may include compute, storage, and connectivity concerns that are specific to data center environments.

For enterprise networks, enterprise administrators manage network intent and operational task intent. Application developers specify application-level intents. End users may specify simpler intents like bandwidth requests for specific uses.

The RFC includes concrete examples for each domain: a carrier wanting to guarantee high bandwidth for premium video customers; a data center wanting to limit VNF load to 50% and network links to 70%; an enterprise wanting hologram objects in video conferences to arrive within 50 ms of each other.

Each domain's taxonomy shows which user types, intent types, scopes, and lifecycle models apply, creating a structured view of what intent means in that domain.
sections.eli5: In a carrier, a customer wants a smooth video experience. An operator wants traffic routed efficiently. In a data center, an administrator wants to keep servers from being overloaded. In an enterprise, people want the video conference to feel synchronized. The taxonomy shows which kinds of intent each group uses.
